NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The proposed intervention is to install electrochemical anti-fouling units on the stainless steel plate heat exchanger's inlet and outlet headers to create an electric field that prevents biofilm and scale formation. Standard practice relies on mechanical cleaning and/or chemical treatment (chlorination) to manage fouling, which is both labor-intensive and environmentally constrained. This intervention is a genuine departure because it uses an electrochemical mechanism to disrupt cell attachment and scale nucleation at the molecular level, rather than relying on physical removal or biocidal action. The closest existing practice is cathodic protection in marine environments, but our application differs by using pulsed electric fields specifically tuned to prevent microbial adhesion and scale formation in cooling water systems, not just to prevent corrosion.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory of colloidal stability. The applied electric field increases the energy barrier for particle (bacteria, mineral) attachment to the heat exchanger surfaces by increasing the zeta potential of suspended particles. A 1-3 V/cm electric field can increase the repulsive energy barrier by 5-10 kT, reducing attachment probability by 90-99%. This directly addresses the primary fouling mechanism: initial microbial attachment and subsequent scale formation.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard Practice Bill:
- Mechanical cleaning service (labor, equipment) every 3-6 months
- Chlorination system with residual monitoring
- pH adjustment chemicals

Intervention Bill:
(a) Stainless steel electrode plates (existing material class)
(b) Commercially available pulsed DC power supply (catalog item, e.g., Harwin P-Series)
(b) In-line conductivity probe (existing monitoring equipment class)
(c) Control algorithm adjustment to existing heat exchanger control system (parameter change)
(c) Operating voltage: 1.5 V/cm across plate channels (duty change)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Added: Electrode plates (a) - same burden class as existing heat exchanger plates
- Added: Power supply (b) - same burden class as existing chemical dosing pumps
- Added: Conductivity probe (b) - same burden class as existing water quality sensors
- Added: Control algorithm (c) - no new hardware, same burden as parameter adjustments
- Removed: Mechanical cleaning service - reduced burden
- Removed: Chlorination system - reduced burden
- Removed: pH adjustment chemicals - reduced burden
Net burden: Same or lower (reduced chemical and maintenance costs, minimal added electrical consumption)

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Install electrochemical units on a test heat exchanger in parallel with identical control units. Measure heat transfer coefficient (U-value) and pressure drop weekly for 12 months. Maintain identical flow rates, temperatures, and water chemistry in both units.
Instruments: Heat transfer measurement system (temperature sensors, flow meters), pressure transducers, water quality analyzer.
Pass/Fail Threshold: Test unit must maintain U-value above 2500 W/m²K for 12 months without exceeding 0.5 ppm chlorination. Control unit will experience standard fouling requiring cleaning within 6 months.
Duration: 12 months continuous operation.
Kill Criterion: If test unit U-value drops below 2500 W/m²K at any point before 12 months, or if chlorination exceeds 0.5 ppm residual, the intervention is falsified.
